query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 1 atomic % of aluminum to as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in-situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby significantly reducing oxygen ingress without degrading the alloy’s room-temperature ductility (8–16%) or its high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the as-cast state
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor compositional modification by adding approximately 1 atomic % aluminum
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 1000 °C for approximately 100 hours under mechanical loading corresponding to strain rates of 10^−4 to 10^−2 s^−1
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent, and slow-growing Al2O3 surface layer
generation.mechanism: The added aluminum preferentially oxidizes at high temperature to form a thin, protective Al2O3 scale that acts as a barrier against oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy. This passivation minimizes further oxidation without altering the underlying cast microstructure that governs ductility and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the aluminum-modified alloy is expected to exhibit significantly reduced oxide scale growth (evidenced by lower weight gain and thinner, more adherent oxide layers) while maintaining the target room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated, as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exposed under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-temperature oxidation conditions (1000 °C in air for ~100 hours) and mechanical testing under strain rates ranging from 10^−4 to 10^−2 s^−1; outcomes outside these parameters may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of Al2O3 scale formation, long-term scale adhesion, and any subtle effects on the alloy’s microstructure and mechanical behavior under cyclic or variable loading remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with ~1 atomic % aluminum and a control set without aluminum. Expose both sets to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours while applying mechanical loading corresponding to strain rates of 10^−4 to 10^−2 s^−1. Post-exposure, evaluate the oxide scale characteristics via weight gain measurements, microscopy (SEM/EDS), and XRD, and perform room-temperature tensile tests along with high-temperature yield strength measurements.
measurements: Total weight gain due to oxidation
Oxide layer thickness, morphology, and adhesion (via SEM, EDS, and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar weight gain and oxide scale morphology) compared to the control, or if its measured ductility or yield strength fall outside the acceptable ranges relative to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

frame.system: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the as‐cast state
frame.goal: Enhance high-temperature oxygen resistance while retaining the alloy’s useful ductility and yield strength
frame.limitation: Poor oxygen resistance limits its practical high-temperature use
constraints: A single intervention must be used
The intervention must not sacrifice the alloy’s room‐temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) or its high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C)
The alloy is used in its cast state, so any modification should be applicable in this processing context
frame.regime: Exposure at high temperatures (around 1000 °C) in oxidizing atmospheres (e.g., air) for extended durations (e.g., 100 hours) under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1
prior_attempts: There is no explicit mention of prior alloy modifications such as applying coatings or multi‐element alloying, likely because previous complex interventions compromised mechanical performance or altered the cast microstructure adversely.
frame.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition of a high-oxide‐forming element such as approximately 1 atomic % aluminum into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy will, during high-temperature exposure in an oxidizing environment, lead to the in-situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing, and protective Al2O3 surface layer. This passivation layer should prevent rapid oxygen ingress without significantly altering the alloy’s bulk microstructure and mechanical performance. The proposed intervention would be validated by treating samples at 1000 °C in air for ~100 hours while performing comparative mechanical tests (tensile testing at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) against untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr. A controlled falsification experiment would involve processing an alloy batch identically but without the aluminum addition. If the Al-containing alloy exhibits significantly reduced oxide scale growth (as measured by weight gain and microstructural analysis of the oxide scale) while maintaining comparable ductility and yield strength, it would confirm the hypothesis. Conversely, if oxidation rates remain similar or if mechanical properties degrade, the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early studies on equiatomic refractory or high‐entropy alloys like the Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 system (e.g., PMC5578249) largely focused on processing routes and microstructural control to optimize high-temperature performance, but did not tackle oxidation resistance directly. Later work (e.g., PMC7513042) introduced minor alloying additions—in that case in an HEA containing aluminum—to initiate in-situ formation of stable oxide particles (Al2O3) to improve overall performance under high temperatures. However, while these approaches showed that controlled oxide formation can enhance certain mechanical properties or wear resistance, a dedicated intervention to form a continuous, protective scale without altering the cast microstructure has not yet been attempted.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to overcome the poor oxygen resistance of as-cast HfNbTaTiZr under high-temperature oxidizing conditions without compromising its room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength. Prior methods either modified the processing in ways that induced detrimental secondary phases or used complex multiphase approaches that would risk the cast microstructure.
decision.lever: Introduce a minor addition (~1 atomic %) of aluminum into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to enable the in-situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing protective Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure in air (around 1000 °C for ~100 hours) under relevant strain rates.
decision.why: This step directly follows the trend seen in analogous systems where small amounts of a high-oxide-forming element (as in PMC7513042) facilitate the precipitation of a protective oxide without altering bulk mechanical properties. It addresses the identified gap by using a compositional modification that can improve oxidation resistance while preserving the alloy’s as-cast ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
